anomaly_def.Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Page-level serialization inside the buffer manager where sessions compete for latches, pins, or hot pages, stalling access even though memory is available.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space reaches its hard limit, preventing further data-file, log, or temp-area growth and returning allocation-failed errors.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume nearly all host CPU cycles, pushing run-queue length and context-switch rates to saturation.

When all three root causes arise together, the system exhibits a compound failure pattern: intense latch waits and buffer-busy events are interleaved with repeated allocation-failed errors while overall response time is further stretched by CPU starvation. Hot pages spin on latches yet cannot be evicted or flushed because datafiles or redo/archive destinations have no free space, causing dirty-page flush threads to loop futilely and burn CPU. Concurrent sessions observe a mixture of page-latch, space-allocation, and scheduler-related wait events, prolonged commit latency (logs cannot extend), surging spin CPU without throughput gain, and sudden statement failures once space or CPU is fully exhausted.

Causally, space exhaustion blocks checkpoints and background writers from completing, keeping dirty pages resident. These pages amplify latch contention because they cannot be flushed and released, lengthening hold times on buffer latches. The extended latch hold times drive up CPU utilization as sessions spin or context-switch while waiting, pushing the host toward CPU saturation. In turn, a saturated CPU slows the very maintenance tasks (file growth, log archival, buffer flush) needed to resolve space shortages and clear dirty pages, completing a feedback loop that escalates all three anomalies and can lead to widespread throughput collapse or instance hang.

entry.official_definition: The execution timeout for SELECT statements, in milliseconds.
entry.trigger_condition: A SELECT statement exceeds the configured max_execution_time limit.
entry.workload_impact: The SELECT statement is interrupted by the execution time limit.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when statement execution exceeds a configured execution-time budget because the operation runs too long or the workload is blocked behind other work.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect query shape, access path quality, resource contention, and whether the timeout threshold should be reviewed together with the workload pattern.
